1: # HGSS 3DS: debugging an optimized DS port
2: 
3: The HeartGold/SoulSilver port translates DS graphics and audio to 3DS software and GPU operations. Its worklogs show that a locally correct optimization can be inactive, slower in a real scene, or unsafe when another part of the pipeline changes state. This case study records specific failures and the checks that exposed them; it is not a benchmark for other games.
4: 
5: ## Before you start
6: 
7: The entries below are the project's own reports, not measurements reproduced by Coffeepot. They describe particular development builds and scenes on Old 3DS or, where explicitly stated, Azahar or a host. Firmware, exact toolchain and run conditions are not consistently stated in the notes. The original worklogs are linked at revision `845cae5`; newer P2–P4 findings are at revision `443a22f`. Both commits are ancestors of the public `main` branch of the HGSS repository and, on November 11, 2026, both resolved through GitHub's commit API and raw-file URLs (an earlier audit that day could not retrieve them; if a link fails again, the full hashes in the URLs identify the commits to restore from a fork or archive). Numbers from different sessions or renderer configurations must not be combined into a single before/after result.
8: 
9: ## Establish the bottleneck and validate the counters
10: 
11: On November 10, 2026, two Old 3DS Goldenrod field runs of builds `b3024a0` and `b3024a0-profoff` reported 8.6–9.8 compositions/s, 4.0–5.5 publishes/s and drawer wall times of 92–179 ms. The project identified the drawer as the presentation constraint in those runs. The two logs were not an acceptable matched PROFILE/OFF A/B; do not infer instrumentation overhead from their difference. [reported: HGSS baseline worklog, firmware and full conditions not stated]
12: 
13: A geometry throttle was built from an apparent 27-built-to-6-shown ratio, but `sSwapsDone` also counted skipped scenes. The first throttle serialized producer and consumer; the project reported Azahar compositions falling from 23.75 to 11.50/s. Both throttle variants were reverted. [reported: HGSS pacing worklog, November 10, 2026; Azahar, version and test model unspecified] The fix was not another throttle: inspect every counter's increment sites and relate a change to the stage that limits the chosen output metric.
14: 
15: Another counter used an unsigned 64-bit accumulator as `total -= start; ...; total += end`. A different thread could sample the intermediate negative value as a huge positive duration. Measure the interval in a local variable and publish a complete sample with appropriate synchronization. Also distinguish nested timers: the project's `take` interval already contained flat-fill and object-sort intervals. Adding all three counted the same time more than once. Thread wall time includes waiting and preemption; it is not automatically CPU time. See [performance](../performance.md#measuring-time).
16: 
17: ## Fast paths: prove admission, work and output separately
18: 
19: A band-redraw fixture reported bit-exact results and fewer visited scanlines, but an in-game Goldenrod menu smoke recorded zero object-band and background-band takes. Build flags had also initially reached application compilation but not the library containing the optimized code; several emulator runs had tested the off-path. The team added build identifiers, invalidation markers, symbol checks and admission/rejection counters. [reported: HGSS wave-2 integration, November 6, 2026; host fixtures and Azahar, not an Old 3DS timing result]
20: 
21: The P3 flat-picture skip first recorded zero skips in a 600-tick Azahar field window. Later per-field diagnostics attributed a changing byte on every pass to the low byte of `VCOUNT`; the project excluded the timing fields from this *rendered-picture* signature and reported the skip engaging in that scene. This is a project-specific result, not permission to omit display timing or interrupt state from emulation: interrupt-driven writes can change effective visual state. [reported: HGSS November 2026 P3 worklog, Azahar 2126.2 Old 3DS profile; not a hardware result] Track attempts, takes, rejection reasons, work avoided and output disagreements. A green fixture and a zero-hit live path establish different things.
22: 
23: The same worklog describes a post-draw hash that could label an old rendered picture with newer live VRAM contents. The project moved its retained signature before drawing, which prevents that particular association error but does not guarantee a coherent image if VRAM changes during the draw. In two reported 600-tick Azahar windows (field at rest and walking), three draws were hashed before and after and no hash difference was observed. Three matching pairs do not establish that no write occurred, rule out A → B → A, or establish a hardware race rate. [reported: HGSS P3/P4 worklog, build `9759707`; Azahar, not hardware] A coherent snapshot or equivalent synchronization remains necessary; see [visual-state signatures](../PICA200/rendering-2d.md#cache-effective-visual-state-not-raw-register-blocks).
24: 
25: In a separate P2 experiment, four geometry optimizations engaged and audits passed, yet the combined configuration reduced Azahar compositions by 28–33% in the specified scripts; the team reverted the bundle. [reported: HGSS P2 results at revision `443a22f`, November 2026; Azahar 2126.2 Old 3DS profile, not hardware] This establishes a regression for that bundle and test, not which individual flag caused it or what it would cost on hardware.
26: 
27: ## State lifetime and batch boundaries
28: 
29: A retained sorted-object list survived when DS object rendering was disabled. Normal software sprite drawing checked the enable bit, but GPU admission and an empty-plane shortcut consumed the old count. The fix cleared the retained count on disable; a fixture exercised enable → disable without clearing object memory → re-enable and compared the actual renderer with a forced full render. It reproduced the bug locally; the note does not prove that stale count was the cause of the corresponding hardware performance result. [reported: HGSS run 26 note, November 2026; host fixture, hardware attribution unconfirmed]
30: 
31: A different optimization merged opaque 3D batches and changed stencil handling. Characters appeared duplicated and halos appeared around effects on both Old 3DS and New 3DS. The worklog traces the regression to changed vertex ranges and state dependencies, and reports reverting the merge and stencil change while retaining separate state caching and texture hoisting. [reported: HGSS session 20, November 2026; exact builds and scene conditions in that note] A batch boundary needs equivalent textures, vertex ranges, depth, stencil, blend and ordering semantics, not just matching material labels. A scene that looks like a sprite bug may originate in 3D: inspect the source object table and the actual submitted geometry before assigning ownership.
32: 
33: The battle dialogue mirror is another useful boundary: the GPU background take ran in a command phase where blending was off, but a blended entry phase used the software path. The team replaced a dead overlay-name veto with a battle-state veto; Azahar showed correct text with that workaround. The underlying GPU mirror mechanism and the hardware A/B of the veto were still open in the pinned note. [reported: HGSS W2, November 4, 2026; pre-fix mirror confirmed on Old 3DS] Capture registers, all relevant graphics memory, palettes and object state from the *same phase*, including prior output-buffer contents. An uncaptured dependency or a screenshot taken seconds later is not a valid comparison.
34: 
35: ## Interrupts, callbacks and shutdown
36: 
37: The port's emulated H-blank walk dispatched 192 line events; a thread switch was requested after each. In one Old 3DS session the project attributed roughly 12 ms of a frame to the interrupt phase, then reported 12,751 → 411 µs after deferring the switches until the end of the walk while retaining handlers and bookkeeping. [reported: HGSS session 20, November 2026; exact builds, firmware and complete run conditions not specified] This is not a general license to defer interrupts: verify handler ordering, visibility and any code that depends on a switch between events. Time dispatch, work and scheduling separately before changing them.
38: 
39: The Settings callback example is a lifetime failure: a V-blank callback could run after its background configuration had been freed. The port-specific fix disabled the callback before freeing the object; the scripted PC reproduction passed, with hardware acceptance tracked separately. Another shutdown hung because the geometry worker was joined before a queue drain that required that worker. Drain while the consumer still runs, then stop and join it; do not free a thread after a timed-out join. These are project-specific dependencies—draw your own ownership and shutdown graph. See [thread lifetime](../threading.md#thread-lifetime) and [lifecycle](../application-lifecycle.md#exit).
40: 
41: ## Audio and save compatibility failures
42: 
43: The port's linker placed an empty section alias away from the intended volume table. The game then interpreted unrelated data as fader values; notes describe stuck, over-loud channels. A replacement table and link-time checks fixed the diagnosed alias, but a later correction expanded it from 128 to 256 entries after an in-game index of 128 exposed the first fix as incomplete. A clean PC waveform still did not prove the DSP handoff: the project separately found an unflushed audio buffer. Validate table bounds against all real callers, compare samples before and after mixing, and check buffer ownership and cache flush at the DSP boundary. [reported: HGSS S13, November 2026; host audio comparisons, later device symptoms; full conditions in source] Apply headroom before saturation; turning down an already clipped signal does not recover it. See [audio](../audio.md#diagnosing-crackles-and-gaps).
44: 
45: A different compatibility layer paired a reflected CRC table with a non-reflected update algorithm. The port could read its own wrongly checksummed saves while rejecting retail saves. The repair used the correct table and recognized the known legacy checksum during migration, while still rejecting values matching neither. [reported: HGSS S17, November 2026; host test, device round-trip pending] Check a known vector and independently produced saves in both directions; a self-round-trip alone is insufficient. See [files and saves](../filesystem-and-saves.md#testing-failure-handling).
46: 
47: ## Technical details: reproduce the investigation
48: 
49: 1. Freeze scene, save, script, configuration, binary hash, model and firmware; keep baseline binaries in separate output directories. Compare repeated, alternating A/B runs where possible and record logging overhead separately.
50: 2. Check runtime model and build banners in *each* log. Confirm feature flags reached every library and that the tested binary actually contains and executes the intended path.
51: 3. Define each metric's start/end, unit, denominator and nesting. Reconcile queued, completed, skipped and displayed counts; do not add a child timer to its parent.
52: 4. Capture one coherent graphics state and identical prior buffers. Compare the candidate against an independently forced reference, test invalidation, and verify the fast path fires. A reference implementation can itself be wrong: use an independent capture when both paths share an assumption.
53: 5. Report host and emulator correctness separately from Old 3DS and New 3DS timing, audio, lifecycle and visual checks. A private or dirty-tree note should not be represented as a pinned public revision.
54: 
55: ## Pitfalls and open questions
56: 
57: - A signature may cover the right bytes but race a writer between hashing and rendering. The limited before/after hash observations above do not establish its frequency or a safe general fix.
58: - A `0 disagreements` counter only covers the path, states and fields actually compared. It does not prove a dormant optimization or every graphics mode correct.
59: - One scene or one matched pair cannot establish performance throughout the game; background loads, battle effects and hardware contention change the result.
60: - The pinned project status and claim sheets contain historical entries; consult the dated worklog and exact artifact before treating a gate as complete. Coffeepot has not repeated the runs.
61:

Every page must work for both. ## Repository layout ```text AGENTS.md zensical.toml # site config: navigation, theme, and what is excluded glossary.md # global jargon glossary README.md # human landing page (what this wiki covers) / # one directory per console platform (e.g. ctr/, nx/) index.md # console overview + hub glossary.md # per-device jargon glossary hardware/.md # one page per hardware component/system software/.md # one page per system software / format / service homebrew/.md # one page per exploit / tool / library / workflow engineering/.md # one page per practical problem (debugging, performance, porting...) benchmarks// # buildable benchmark programs + README.md with method and results tools/ check_docs.py # link, anchor and Sources-section checker build_benchmarks.sh # builds every benchmark, fails on warnings site/ # generated site output (not committed) ``` Current scope is three platforms: `ctr/` (Nintendo 3DS family), `nx/` (Nintendo Switch family) and `oz/` (Nintendo Switch 2 family). Add a new top-level platform directory only for a distinct hardware platform, using its established codename or short kebab-case name (e.g. `ctr`, `nx`, `oz`). File names are kebab-case: `arm9-cpu.md`, `nand-filesystem.md`, `boot9strap.md`. One topic per file. ## Core principles 1. **Don't repeat yourself. Link instead.** If something is already explained on another page, summarize it in at most 1–2 sentences and link to the canonical page. Never copy a full explanation into two places. 2. **Write like a human.** Natural, plain language first. Short paragraphs. Active voice. A motivated non-expert should be able to follow the Overview of any page. 3. **Minimal jargon, full technical detail.** Avoid jargon unless it names something precisely. When jargon is necessary, define it once, link it to a glossary, then use it freely. Never simplify away technical facts (registers, addresses, versions, file offsets, behaviors) to sound readable — push them into a `Technical details` section instead of dropping them. 4. **Progressive disclosure.** Plain-language summary up top, exhaustive detail below. Human reads the top; agent reads the whole page. ## Jargon and glossaries Jargon means any term a non-expert would stumble on: acronyms (`SoC`, `IPC`), Nintendo-specific codenames (`CTR`, `Horizon`), homebrew terms (`CFW`, `ROP`), and hardware terms used in a precise sense (`physical address`, `kernel privilege`). Rules: - On first use in a page, give the plain meaning, then the term in bold with a glossary link. Example: `the main chip that combines CPU and GPU (a **system-on-a-chip**, or **[SoC](../../glossary.md#soc)**)`. After that, just use `SoC`. - Every jargon term used on a page must resolve to exactly one glossary entry: either the global glossary or that console's glossary. - **Global `glossary.md`**: terms with the same meaning across two or more consoles, or general computing terms (`CPU`, `GPU`, `kernel`, `firmware`, `NAND`, `ARM`). Define once here. - **Per-device `/glossary.md`**: terms specific to one console (`boot9strap`, `Horizon`, `PICA200`). Define here. - If a per-device term starts being used by pages for a second console with the same meaning, promote it to the global glossary and leave a pointer link behind in the per-device glossary. - Glossary entries are short: 1–4 sentences of plain meaning, plus the precise technical sense in one more sentence if needed, plus a link to the canonical wiki page for the full story. Never put the full explanation in the glossary; the glossary points at pages, pages point back at the glossary. Glossary entry format: ```markdown ### Term name One to four sentences: what it is in plain language, then the precise sense. Ends with a link to the canonical page. Example: ### System-on-a-chip (SoC) ``` ## Page types Pick exactly one type per page. If a topic spans types (e.g. a chip and its SDK driver), split into linked pages rather than one blended page. - `/index.md` — console overview and hub. What the console is, when it was sold, what makes it distinctive, spec summary (as a table of links, not raw numbers repeated from subpages), software landscape, homebrew state. Links to every major subpage. - `hardware/.md` — one hardware component or subsystem (CPU, GPU, memory map, display, input, cartridge, wireless). What it does, where it sits in the system, its observable behavior, then full specs. - `software/.md` — one software thing (OS/kernel, system menu, applet, file format, filesystem, system service, update mechanism). What the user sees, what a developer needs to know, formats and behaviors. - `homebrew/.md` — one exploit, custom firmware, tool, library, or workflow. What it achieves, who it is for, how it works, how to use it, limits and risks. - `engineering/.md` — one practical problem a developer faces when writing software for the console (debugging, profiling, performance, memory management, rendering, asset conversion, hardware testing). Reference pages say what the hardware and libraries *are*; engineering pages say how to *use* them in working software and how to check the result. They link to the reference pages for facts rather than restating them. ## Templates Copy the matching template. Delete sections that genuinely don't apply, but never delete `Technical details` or `Sources` — if detail is unknown, say what is unknown. ### Console index ```markdown # Plain-language overview: what this console is, when it was sold, what makes it notable. 3–6 sentences. ## At a glance | Area | Summary | | ---- | ------- | | CPU | [One-line plain summary](hardware/.md) | | GPU / video | [One-line plain summary](hardware/.md) | | Memory | [One-line plain summary](hardware/.md) | | Storage / media | [One-line plain summary](hardware/.md) | | Operating software | [One-line plain summary](software/.md) | | Homebrew status | 1–2 sentences + link to key [homebrew page](homebrew/.md) | Keep numbers out of this table unless they fit in one line. Full specs live on subpages. ## Hardware Bulleted list of subpages with one plain sentence each: [Page](hardware/.md) — what it covers. ## Software Same: [Page](software/.md) — what it covers. ## Homebrew Same: [Page](homebrew/.md) — what it achieves and who it is for. ## Notes and open questions Anything uncertain, disputed, or TODO. Be explicit: what is unknown, what would answer it. ## Sources - [Title](URL) — what this source covers ``` ### Hardware page ```markdown # Plain-language overview: what this part does and why it matters. 3–6 sentences. No unexplained acronyms here. ## Where it fits How this component connects to the rest of the system (1 short paragraph + links to neighboring pages). Example: CPU reads from X, sends display lists to [GPU](gpu.md). ## How it works Observable behavior in plain language: what software can make it do, what the user would notice. Link jargon to glossaries on first use. ## Technical details Full detail for agent work: models, revisions, clock speeds, registers, addresses, memory maps, timing, quirks, revision differences. Use tables for registers/specs. Do not simplify here. If a value differs by model or firmware, give the table, not a single number. ## Homebrew notes What a homebrew developer needs: how to access this hardware, what libraries/registers/services expose it, common pitfalls. 1–2 sentences + links if the full workflow lives on a [homebrew page](../homebrew/.md). ## Sources - [Title](URL) — what this source covers ``` ### Software page ```markdown # Plain-language overview: what the user sees, what it is for. 3–6 sentences. ## Behavior What it does, when it runs, how it interacts with other software/hardware. Keep historical and technical explanations of exploits, bootloaders and firmware. Never assume a New 3DS. Anything that applies only to the New 3DS, or that differs on it, goes in an explicit **New 3DS** disclaimer after the Old 3DS statement. - **Terminology.** Use exactly "Old 3DS" and "New 3DS" (capitalised, with the space). "All models" means both. Do not use "O3DS", "N3DS", "original 3DS", "3DS XL" or "New Nintendo 3DS" as model labels. Mention the 2DS, 2DS XL or other variants only where they differ in a way that matters, and then name them in the disclaimer. - **Disclaimer format.** Inline: end the sentence or bullet with `**New 3DS:** .` Block: a blockquote starting `> **New 3DS:**`. In tables with a New 3DS column or row, label it `New 3DS` and keep the Old 3DS column first. - **Not a default.** Never write a New 3DS value as the plain statement ("the CPU runs at 804 MHz", "up to 124 MB"). A code example's verification status lists Old 3DS and New 3DS separately, and an example that uses New 3DS-only features says so up front. - **Code.** Examples must work on an Old 3DS. New 3DS-only calls are guarded by a model check and described in a disclaimer. - Hardware pages describing a New 3DS-only component (for example the extra CPU cores, the C-Stick or MVD) say so in the first paragraph. ## Evidence labels Engineering pages, and any performance or behaviour claim elsewhere, must say what supports each non-obvious claim. Tag it inline with one of: | Label | Meaning | | ----- | ------- | | `[documented]` | Stated in official documentation or readable in the source code of the library/firmware involved (name the file) | | `[reverse-engineered]` | Established through reverse engineering or hardware experiments published by others (name who) | | `[measured]` | A benchmark result; give console model, firmware/CFW version, build, and conditions | | `[reported]` | A measurement or claim published by a third party that this wiki has not reproduced (developer postmortem, port README, interview, talk). Name the source and its date, the console model, and the conditions as stated; say when the source does not state them. Never present a `[reported]` figure as `[measured]`, and never extend it to other workloads or models | | `[hypothesis]` | Plausible but unverified; say what would confirm or refute it | Never let a `[hypothesis]` or `[reported]` lose its label when it is copied to another page. Advice like "X is faster" without a `[measured]` result or a `[documented]` mechanism behind it does not belong in the wiki. Code examples must state what they were checked against: at minimum, that they compile with a named toolchain/library version. Say explicitly when an example has not been run on hardware. ## Code, benchmarks and verification - Every code example and benchmark carries a **verification status**: *builds* (with the toolchain versions on the console's source-versions page, no warnings under `-Wall`), *emulator-tested*, *Old 3DS-tested*, *New 3DS-tested*. Record it in the console's source-versions page (CTR: `ctr/engineering/source-versions.md`) and, for benchmarks, in `benchmarks/README.md`. Their README states the question, the method, the variants to run, and how to record results. Raw results go in the README; the page whose claim they settle gets the `[measured]` label and a link. - Emulator timings are never results. - When a claim depends on a library or firmware version, pin it: record the commit on the source-versions page and link the source file at that commit when the exact behaviour matters. - **When new results arrive, update every page that states the old status.** `tools/check_docs.py` keeps a list of stale status phrases (`STALE_PHRASES`): when a status changes (something is now measured, run, or compared), add the old wording to that list so a page that still repeats it fails the check. `python3 tools/check_docs.py --external` also fetches every external link; CI runs it as an informational job so a citation that stops resolving gets noticed. - Emulator checks (`tools/emu_pixel_check.py`, `tools/emu_smoke.py`) are recorded as `emulator-tested` for what they establish (a picture matches, a program finishes) and never as timing; the benchmark README says what each one did and did not exercise. - Run `python3 tools/check_docs.py` and `zensical build --strict` (and `tools/build_benchmarks.sh` if code changed) before committing. Readers and agents should always know where the precise facts are. - **Define before use.** Never use an acronym or codename without its plain meaning + glossary link on first use per page. - **Link aggressively.** At least: first mention of any wiki-covered topic links to its page; first mention of any jargon links to its glossary entry; spec tables link outward rather than duplicating numbers. Use relative links (`../software/os.md`, `../../glossary.md#term` from a `hardware/` or `software/` page). - **Cite sources.** Every page ends with Sources. Prefer primary sources (hardware manuals, leaked SDK docs where legally usable, upstream repos, reputable console wikis with verification). Note what each source was used for. - **State uncertainty explicitly.** Use `Notes and open questions` or inline `> Unknown:` callouts. Never present a guess as fact. Record the firmware/model/revision a fact was verified against where it matters. - **Keep it readable.** Short paragraphs, one idea per paragraph, tables for specs, code blocks or hex tables for layouts. No walls of unexplained hex. - **No placeholders.** Don't create a page that is only headings. If research is thin, write the Overview + what is known + open questions, and say so. ## The site (zensical) The wiki is published as a static site with [zensical](https://zensical.org/), configured in `zensical.toml`. The site is the wiki: `docs_dir` is the repository root, so every Markdown page in the repository is a wiki page, and the rendered output is written to `site/`. ```bash pip install zensical zensical serve # live preview on http://localhost:8000/coffeepot/ zensical build --clean # write the static site to site/ zensical build --strict # same, but fail the build on a broken link or anchor ``` - **Navigation is explicit.** `nav` in `zensical.toml` lists every page, in the order a reader should meet it. The console `index.md` pages carry the same curated order; keep the two in step. - **A new page must be added to `nav`.** A page that is not in `nav` is still built, but it is not reachable from the sidebar. - **`exclude_docs` lists what is not a wiki page**: repository plumbing, vendored trees, benchmark build artefacts. Anything added to the repository that is not a page belongs in that list, or it gets published. - **Links between pages use source paths** (`../software/os.md`, `../../glossary.md#soc`). zensical rewrites them to site URLs and validates both the target and the anchor, so a broken link fails `zensical build --strict`. - `site/` is generated output and is not committed. ## Agent workflow 1. Before writing, search the wiki for existing coverage (`hardware/`, `software/`, `homebrew/`, both glossaries). If a canonical page exists, link to it — don't fork the explanation. 2.
